summary: Adds a location parameter for ISUP cause values in the SIP Reason header field (RFC 3326), so services can tell where in the phone network a call was released. It updates RFC 3326 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a call ends, this note says which part of the phone system ended it.

questions: what is the sip reason location parameter
what does location ln mean in sip reason header
how does sip carry q.850 location
subtitle: A small SIP extension that says where in the phone network a call was released.

tldr.problem: The SIP Reason header field can carry an ISUP (Q.850) cause value saying why a call ended, but not the Q.850 location saying which part of the network released it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8606 adds a location parameter to the Reason header field, with 16 named values such as U, LN, TN and INTL that map to the 4-bit Q.850 location.
tldr.outcome: Services in SIP networks can now interpret a release reason together with where it happened. The document updates RFC 3326 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8606 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It updates RFC 3326 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why a Location Is Needed
sections.content:
The SIP Reason header field, defined in RFC 3326, tells why a SIP dialog or an interworked PSTN call ended. The reason can be a SIP response or an ISUP release cause as specified in Q.850. RFC 6432 lets a Q.850 cause code ride in a SIP response, but it does not carry the Q.850 location, which identifies the part of the ISUP network where the call was released.

Some services need that location to interpret the reason correctly. RFC 8606 adds a location value to the reason-extension parameter of RFC 3326 so the value can be interworked from the PSTN. The gateway only needs to include the location it received.
sections.eli5: Knowing a call ended is one thing. Knowing who hung up it, the caller's side or somewhere in the middle, is extra help.

sections.title: Rationale
sections.content:
The main intended use is in IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) networks defined by 3GPP. The parameter is also open to any other network that has ISUP interworking gateways and uses Q.850 reason codes.

Its job is to hold the location of the call release so it can travel from the originating PSTN entity to the SIP entity in a response or a BYE message.
sections.eli5: It is a label that travels with the hang-up message, so the other end learns where the hang-up came from.

sections.title: The Location Parameter
sections.content:
Under RFC 6432, any SIP response except 100 (Trying) MAY contain a Reason header field with a Q.850 cause code. RFC 8606 adds a location parameter to it. The location is a 4-bit value covering the places where an ISUP call can be released. Some values are spare or reserved for national use.

A UAC or UAS SHALL include the location parameter when it builds a Reason header field with a Q.850 cause and the ISUP location is available. The parameter is only for Q.850 cause values, and in any other case it MUST be ignored if present.

The LOC-* names are the wire codepoints for the values that Q.850 leaves spare or reserved. They stay the wire codepoints if those values are later allocated or used nationally.
sections.eli5: There are sixteen possible places, each with a short code. If the gateway knows the place, it must write the code down.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows a SIP 404 response sent when a gateway receives an ISUP release with Q.850 cause 1, Unallocated (unassigned) number, meaning the number is not known in the PSTN. Its Reason header field reads Q.850;cause=1;text="Unallocated (unassigned) number";location=LN.

Here LN says the call was released in the public network serving the local user.
sections.eli5: A reply says 'that number does not exist', and the added note says which network figured that out.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The location provides little more exposure than the Q.850 cause itself. It does not reveal who the calling or called party is, and it does not show anyone's physical location. It shows only the ISUP network location of the device that released the call.

The document changes none of the security considerations of RFC 3326, and RFC 3398 covers the security issues of ISUP and SIP interworking. The RFC argues that the location is very imprecise, so it adds no major security constraints and does not make fraud easier.
sections.eli5: The note says which part of the phone system ended the call. It does not say where any person is.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA has registered a new SIP header parameter in the Header Field Parameters and Parameter Values subregistry of the SIP Parameters registry. The header field is Reason, the parameter name is location, predefined values are Yes, and the reference is RFC 8606.
sections.eli5: The new label was written into the official list of SIP labels so everyone uses the same name.

items.label: LPN
items.desc: Private network serving the local user.

items.label: LN
items.desc: Public network serving the local user.

items.label: RLN
items.desc: Public network serving the remote user.

items.label: RPN
items.desc: Private network serving the remote user.
